title: Bus
body:
A shared bundle of parallel wires connecting the [[CPU]], [[Main memory]], and the support
chips. Shared is the point and the problem: only one device can drive it at a time, so
somebody has to arbitrate (on the Atari ST that is [[GLUE]]), and the [[VonNeumann]]
bottleneck is exactly this contention.

Three buses, by what they carry:

## Address bus

Which location. Driven by the CPU (or by whatever has been granted the bus, see
[[Direct Memory Access]]), one wire per address bit, so its width sets how much memory can
exist at all: $n$ lines address $2^n$ locations. The 68000 brings out 24 lines for 16MB,
though the course's machine only populates part of that, which is what makes an access
"outside addressable memory" a bus error.

## Data bus

The actual bits. Bidirectional, because a read and a write both use it. The 68000's is 16
bits wide, which is why it is called a 16-bit processor despite having 32-bit registers, and
why a longword access takes two bus cycles. It is also why a word access at an odd address
is an address error: the hardware fetches aligned 16-bit chunks and cannot straddle.

## Control bus

Everything else: read or write, the [[Clock]], bus grant and acknowledge, and the interrupt
lines the [[68901 MFP]] asserts. Not a coherent bundle so much as the leftovers, but it is
what turns two piles of wires into a protocol.
